'''Dinengdeng''', also known as '''inabráw''', is a traditional [[Filipino cuisine|Filipino vegetable-based dish]]. It is characterized by a savory and earthy flavor, largely derived from fermented [[anchovy]] fish sauce (''buggúong'' or ''[[Bagoong|bagoong isda]]''), which provides a distinct salty [[umami]] taste.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gaioni, Dominic T., & |first1=Kenneth Kahn |title=Health and nutrition in a Philippine highland community |journal=Nutrition and Health |date=2002 |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=255–266 |doi=10.1177/026010600201600401 |pmid=12617278 |s2cid=41934520 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=News |first= |date=2017 |title=Ilocano vegetable dishes, ihahain sa 'Pinas Sarap' |url=https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/newstv/pinassarap/625385/ilocano-vegetable-dishes-ihahain-sa-pinas-sarap/story/ |access-date=2026-01-15 |website=GMA News Online |language=en}}</ref> The dish typically includes a combination of lowland [[Vegetable|vegetables]]—such as leaves, fruits, flowers, and [[Legume|legumes]]—like [[okra]], [[Asparagus bean|long beans]], [[eggplant]], [[Moringa oleifera|moringa leaves]], [[Momordica charantia|bitter gourd]], and [[Corchorus olitorius|jute leaves]], and may be cooked with grilled or fried fish or [[dried shrimp]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Astudillo |first=Rene |date=2019-01-08 |title=The Happy Home Cook: Dinengdeng With Fried Bangus |url=https://www.positivelyfilipino.com/magazine/the-happy-home-cook-dinengdeng-with-fried-bangus |access-date=2026-01-15 |website=Positively Filipino {{!}} Online Magazine for Filipinos in the Diaspora |language=en-US}}</ref> It is commonly served as a main course and eaten with [[Cooked rice|steamed rice]]. Originating from the [[Ilocos Region]] of northwestern [[Luzon]], [[Philippines]], it remains a staple of [[Ilocano cuisine]].<ref name="WuCheung2002">{{cite book|author1=David Yen Ho Wu|author2=Sidney C. H. Cheung|title=Wu: Globalization of Chinese Food|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pmGoXCmdIdIC&pg=PA183|access-date=March 24, 2013|year=2002|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-2582-9|page=183}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Dinengdeng (Inabraw) Recipe {{!}} NAPC® {{!}} Nestlé Goodnes PH |url=https://www.nestlegoodnes.com/ph/recipes/dinengdeng-inabraw |access-date=2026-01-15 |website=www.nestlegoodnes.com |language=en}}</ref>

Dinengdeng has numerous regional and seasonal variations, depending on the combination of vegetables used.<ref>{{Cite web |last=NewsPublish |date=2024-03-15 |title=A ‘dinengdeng’ diary |url=https://lifestyle.inquirer.net/485945/a-dinengdeng-diary/ |access-date=2026-01-15 |website=Lifestyle.INQ |language=en-US}}</ref> ''Buridibod'' is one such variation and is typically prepared with [[sweet potato]] and [[Moringa oleifera|moringa fruit]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dacpano |first=Brenda |date=2013 |title=Makan a la Pinoy: Dinengdeng, inabraw, buridibod, baradibod |url=https://nordis.net/2013/01/13/article/opinion/columns/makan/makan-a-la-pinoy-dinengdeng-inabraw-buridibod-baradibod/ |website=Northern Dispatch}}</ref> [[Pinakbet]] is a related dish prepared with similar vegetables but less liquid.<ref>{{cite web |title=A Taste of Ilocos Norte |url=https://museoilocosnorte.com/ilocos-norte/information/a-taste-of-ilocos-norte/ |website=Museo Ilocos Norte |date=9 December 2008}}</ref> Dinengdeng is also comparable to [[sinabawang gulay]], bulanglang, and laswa, which typically use [[salt]] or [[Patis (fish sauce)|patis]] to taste instead of bagoong isda.<ref>{{Cite web |title=PCAARRD urges public to rediscover indigenous veggies {{!}} Philippine News Agency |url=https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1157732 |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20240901143316/https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1157732 |archive-date=2024-09-01 |access-date=2026-01-15 |website=www.pna.gov.ph |language=en}}</ref>
